strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: adapting frozen CLIP retrievers to distribution-shifted queries (multilingual, long-form, multimodal) without costly re-embedding or redeployment.

The core technical insight -- that naive similarity-score rewards cause 'score inflation' by rewarding generic high-frequency tokens, and that a corpus-relative ranking-based reward avoids this failure mode -- is clearly motivated and empirically demonstrated (Fig. 5, Fig. 6, and qualitative examples of the LLM injecting generic words like 'environment').

Broad experimental coverage across three distinct types of distribution shift (multilingual: Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600; length: Wikipedia; modality: CIRR) and three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), with consistent improvements over both vanilla CLIP and frozen-LLM rewriting baselines.

Useful ablations beyond the main table: data-efficiency curves showing GRAPE approaches full-data performance with far fewer training samples, and a per-language breakdown on XM3600 that honestly shows the method's gains are bounded by the underlying LLM's knowledge coverage of low-resource languages.

Qualitative case studies (Figs. 2-3) provide intuitive, concrete illustrations of how GRAPE recovers implicit entities in cross-lingual rewrites, distills/expands long Wikipedia text, and resolves multimodal references that vanilla LLM/VLM rewriting fails at.
Reasonably honest discussion of limitations (LLM knowledge-coverage ceiling, retriever upper bound, inference latency overhead) rather than glossing over them.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the training-free baselines discussed in Related Work (ComCLIP, PlugIR), despite explicitly motivating GRAPE as an improvement over them; the only baselines compared in the main table are vanilla CLIP and a frozen (non-retrieval-supervised) LLM rewriter, which likely understates the difficulty of the true competitive landscape.

Terminology/method naming is inconsistent: Section 4.1 introduces 'CLIP+GRPO-LLM' as a comparison method trained with generic retrieval-based rewards, but Table 1 only shows 'CLIP', '+LLM', and '+GRAPE', leaving it unclear whether GRPO-LLM (similarity-reward variant) is ever reported as a full quantitative baseline across all five datasets rather than only in a single ablation on Flickr30k-CN (Fig. 5/6).

The theoretical contribution in Appendix A.1 (affine invariance of GRPO's relative-advantage normalization) is a straightforward property of z-score standardization and does not by itself explain why ranking-based rewards outperform similarity-based ones in practice beyond the empirical score-inflation argument already given in Section 3.3.

Computational/training cost of the ranking reward is not analyzed: computing rk requires ranking the rewritten query against the entire candidate corpus I for every one of the K rollouts per query during RL training, which could be expensive for large N (e.g., XM3600 has thousands of candidates); the efficiency discussion in Section 5 only addresses inference latency, not this training-time cost or its scaling behavior.

Results are reported as single numbers without variance/confidence intervals or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains, especially on smaller datasets like Wikipedia (2,173 train queries) and CIRR (3,336 train queries).

The method requires labeled query-target pairs for training (to compute ground-truth rank), which is a supervision requirement not clearly flagged as a limitation relative to fully training-free baselines like PlugIR that need no labeled retrieval data.

CIRR results (multimodal) show comparatively modest absolute gains (R@1 ~33% vs. ~30% baseline) and are not benchmarked against dedicated composed-image-retrieval methods (e.g., CIR-specific architectures cited in related work), making it harder to judge how competitive GRAPE is in absolute terms for this setting.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: adapting frozen, deployed CLIP retrievers to distributional shifts (multilingual, long-form, multimodal queries) without costly re-embedding/redeployment.

The core diagnostic finding—that naive similarity-score-based RL fine-tuning of the query rewriter causes 'score inflation' via generic/high-frequency tokens—is a clear and intuitively convincing failure mode, illustrated concretely with a qualitative case study (Fig. 5/6) showing rising similarity alongside falling Recall@1.
The proposed fix (corpus-relative, rank-based reward within a GRPO framework) is simple, cheap to compute, and empirically shown to avoid the inflation artifact while improving ranking metrics.

Experiments span three distinct types of distribution shift (multilingual: Flickr30k-CN/CVLUE/XM3600; length: Wikipedia; modality: CIRR) and three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), with generally consistent relative gains over both the frozen-CLIP and frozen-LLM-rewriting baselines.

Useful supplementary analyses: data-efficiency curves, per-language breakdown on XM3600 highlighting the LLM-knowledge bottleneck, and an honest discussion of limitations (retriever upper bound, LLM knowledge coverage, inference latency).
weaknesses: No empirical comparison to the training-free baselines explicitly discussed in the related work (ComCLIP, PlugIR) or to existing retrained multilingual/long-text CLIP variants (mCLIP, AltCLIP, Long-CLIP, LoTLIP) that are cited as alternatives; the only comparisons are against the paper's own ablations (frozen CLIP, frozen-LLM rewriting), making it impossible to judge whether GRAPE actually advances the state of the art versus simply beating a weak internal baseline.

The 'plug-and-play, no retraining' framing is overstated: GRAPE still requires collecting labeled (query, target-image) training data and running GRPO fine-tuning of the rewriter LLM separately for every new domain/corpus (e.g., 89k–149k training queries per dataset in Table 2), which is itself a substantial engineering and data cost, only shifting the retraining burden from the retriever to the LLM rewriter.

The theoretical justification in Appendix A.1 (affine invariance of the GRPO normalization) is a generic property of mean/std normalization applicable to any affine-transformed reward, including similarity scores; it does not actually explain why rank-based signals are more robust to reward hacking than similarity scores, so the core claim rests almost entirely on a single qualitative case study on one dataset (Flickr30k-CN) rather than systematic analysis.

No statistical significance reporting (single run per configuration, no variance/seeds), and no sensitivity/ablation analysis on key hyperparameters such as group size K, KL coefficient λ, or the additive combination of format and ranking rewards.

Zero-shot CLIP baselines are missing entirely for Flickr30k-CN and CIRR (marked '—'), so the paper cannot show the actual gap GRAPE closes relative to no intervention at all on two of five benchmarks, weakening the completeness of the main results table.
Only one rewriter backbone per modality is tested (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for text, Qwen2-VL-7B for CIRR), so generality of the approach across different LLM scales/families is unverified.
Minor but telling presentation issue: the title itself contains a typo ('GPRO' instead of 'GRPO'), suggesting insufficient proofreading of the final manuscript.

Data-efficiency results (Fig. 4) show that even with 10k training samples the method only reaches ~88-94% of full-data performance, which somewhat undercuts the claimed 'data efficiency' of the approach given the already large full training sets (up to 149k queries).

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: adapting CLIP-based retrieval to distribution shifts (multilingual, long-text, multimodal) without costly re-embedding/retraining, which is valuable for production retrieval systems.

The central technical insight—that naive similarity-based RL rewards lead to 'score inflation' where the LLM learns to inject generic high-frequency tokens that raise similarity without improving true relevance—is well illustrated both empirically (Fig. 5/6, with concrete failure-mode examples) and supported by a simple affine-invariance argument for why rank-based rewards are more robust (Appendix A.1).

Reasonably broad empirical validation: five benchmarks spanning three distinct distribution-shift types (Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600 for multilingual; Wikipedia for length; CIRR for multimodal) and three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), with consistent gains over both vanilla CLIP and CLIP+frozen-LLM rewriting.

Thoughtful additional analyses: data-efficiency curves showing the method converges with modest training data, per-language breakdown on XM3600 revealing the expected dependence on LLM language coverage, and qualitative case studies that make the mechanism intuitive.

Candid discussion of limitations (bounded by LLM's knowledge coverage, bounded by the frozen retriever's capacity, added inference latency), which strengthens the credibility of the claims rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: Weak baseline coverage: despite explicitly discussing training-free competitors (ComCLIP, PlugIR) in related work, the main experiments never compare against them directly; the only baselines are vanilla CLIP and CLIP+frozen-LLM rewriting, making it hard to judge GRAPE's standing relative to existing training-free alternatives.

Inconsistency between the stated comparison methods (CLIP, CLIP+LLM, CLIP+GRPO-LLM) in Section 4.1 and the columns actually reported in Table 1 (baseline, +LLM, +GRAPE); it is unclear whether '+GRAPE' is identical to the described 'CLIP+GRPO-LLM' or a distinct, improved variant, and no simpler SFT-style finetuning baseline (e.g., supervised distillation toward the best-ranked rewrite) is included to justify the RL formulation over simpler alternatives.
No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported, so the statistical reliability of the reported gains (e.g., 4.9% average R@10 improvement) cannot be assessed.

The ranking reward requires computing similarity against the full candidate corpus at every rollout step during training, which raises scalability concerns for large corpora; this cost, along with the acknowledged inference-time latency from query rewriting, is not quantified (e.g., wall-clock overhead, throughput impact) despite being flagged as a limitation.

CIRR is evaluated under a custom 80/20 split rather than the standard protocol, and the rewriter model differs across tasks (Qwen2.5-3B vs. Qwen2-VL-7B for CIRR), which complicates direct comparability with prior reported numbers and across the paper's own benchmarks.

The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely consists of applying an existing RL algorithm (GRPO) with a rank-to-reward reformulation of an otherwise standard retrieval reward, rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms for the stated goal.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: bridging distributional shift between downstream queries and CLIP's pretraining distribution without costly retriever retraining or corpus re-embedding.

The identification of the 'score inflation' phenomenon under naive similarity-based reward finetuning is a clear and interesting empirical observation, well illustrated with qualitative examples (Fig. 5) and reward-vs-recall curves (Fig. 6).

The proposed ranking-based reward is theoretically well-motivated via a simple decomposition argument (shared corpus mean cancels out in relative comparisons) and an affine-invariance analysis showing the GRPO advantage is robust to monotonic reward transformations.

Broad empirical coverage across three qualitatively different distribution shifts (multilingual: Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600; long-form: Wikipedia; multimodal: CIRR) and three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), showing consistent gains.

Useful ablations: data efficiency (recovering most performance with 10% of data), group size sensitivity, failure-mode audit (14%→3% failure rate reduction), comparison with strong training-free LLM/VLM rewriting baselines and PlugIR.

Honest and specific discussion of limitations (LLM knowledge bottleneck for low-resource languages, retriever-dependent performance ceiling, inference latency overhead), including a per-language breakdown (Fig. 7) that substantiates the claimed bottleneck.
weaknesses: Baseline CLIP zero-shot results are missing ('—') for Flickr30k-CN and CVLUE in the main results table, without clear explanation; this weakens the ability to judge the absolute magnitude of improvement over the true retriever baseline for two of the five benchmarks.

Results appear to be single-run point estimates with no variance/error bars or significance testing, despite GRPO training being known to have run-to-run variability; this makes it hard to assess how reliable the reported 4.9% average gain is.

The policy-gradient objective in Eq. 3 writes log πθ(r_k | q, C), i.e. conditioning the log-probability on the rank r_k rather than on the generated rewrite q̃_k; this notation appears to be an error/typo that obscures the actual optimization objective and should be corrected for clarity and reproducibility.

The theoretical 'why ranking beats score' argument (Appendix A.1) relies on a simplified linear/additive decomposition of image features (z = μ + z̃) and a linear query-embedding inner product, which is a strong simplification of CLIP's actual learned representation geometry; the practical relevance of this idealized analysis to the real ranking reward's effectiveness is asserted rather than rigorously connected.

Comparisons with other RL/preference-optimization alternatives for query rewriting (e.g., DPO or REINFORCE-style baselines using similarity or rank-based signals other than GRPO) are absent, making it unclear whether the gains are specifically attributable to GRPO's grouped structure versus RL-based finetuning with ranking supervision in general.

The main paper's baselines are limited to CLIP, CLIP+LLM (zero-shot), and CLIP+GRPO-LLM; stronger training-free comparisons (PlugIR, frontier LLM rewriters) are relegated to a small appendix table on only two datasets, understating how the method compares broadly against strong alternatives.

Training cost/compute of the GRPO finetuning stage itself (GPU-hours, number of retrieval calls per step given K rewrites × N candidates) is not reported, which limits reproducibility and understanding of the practical training overhead trade-off.

For the CIRR multimodal setting, the mechanics of computing ranking rewards when a VLM (Qwen2-VL-7B) jointly encodes image+text queries and how this interacts with the same CLIP-frozen retrieval and reward pipeline used for text-only settings are not clearly detailed.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important problem: improving frozen CLIP retrieval under distribution shift without costly retraining/re-embedding, which has clear industrial relevance.

The identification of a 'score inflation' failure mode when naively using similarity as a GRPO reward is a reasonable and intuitively compelling observation, illustrated with a concrete qualitative case (Fig. 5) where the policy learns to append generic phrases to inflate cosine similarity without improving rank.

The experimental scope is broad, covering multilingual, long-text, and compositional multimodal benchmarks, and includes several ablations (data efficiency, group size K, per-language breakdown) that attempt to probe where the method helps and where it is bottlenecked.
The paper is transparent about several limitations (LLM knowledge bottleneck, retriever ceiling, inference latency), which is commendable.
weaknesses: The core policy-optimization objective in Eq. 3 is written as E[log πθ(rk | q, C)], i.e., it appears to condition the log-probability on the rank rk rather than on the generated rewrite q̃k. As written this is either a typo or reflects a conceptual confusion about what the GRPO policy gradient should optimize (the probability of the generated text, not the rank which is a scalar outcome of retrieval). This is a central equation of the method and its presentation undermines confidence in the soundness of the implementation.

The 'baseline' CLIP rows for Flickr30k-CN and CIRR are marked '–' with the explanation that CLIP 'is not capable of handling the task directly.' This is questionable: standard CLIP can still be evaluated zero-shot on Chinese or on text-only CIRR queries (ignoring the image or using straightforward concatenation), and omitting these numbers inflates the apparent necessity of LLM rewriting/GRAPE and prevents a fair before/after comparison.

Comparisons are narrow: the main results table only contrasts CLIP, CLIP+LLM, and CLIP+GRAPE; there is no comparison against other trained query-rewriting approaches (e.g., SFT on retrieval-derived labels, DPO, standard PPO, listwise/pairwise ranking losses) that would isolate the specific benefit of the proposed 'ranking' reward versus simply having *any* retrieval-grounded supervision signal.

Appendix A.3 compares against models named 'Claude-Sonnet-4.6' and 'GPT-5.4,' which do not correspond to any publicly documented model releases; this raises serious concerns about the provenance and reliability of this baseline comparison and, by extension, about the care taken in reporting other experimental results.

The theoretical justification in Appendix A.1 for why ranking rewards outperform similarity rewards is largely a restatement of algebraic identities (z = μ + z̃, q^Tz = q^Tμ + q^Tz̃) rather than a rigorous argument connecting this decomposition to why an RL-trained LLM rewriter would specifically learn to exploit the shared-mean term; it does not constitute a proof and the claimed 'score inflation' mechanism remains primarily empirical/anecdotal (a handful of qualitative examples).

No variance/standard deviation across seeds or significance testing is reported for any of the main Recall@1/@10 numbers, despite several reported gains being modest (e.g., CVLUE R@1 improvements of 1–2.5 points), making it hard to assess whether improvements are robust or within noise.

The ranking reward requires computing the rank of the target among all N corpus candidates for every one of the K rewrites at every training step, which is a nontrivial computational cost; this is in tension with the paper's motivating argument against the 'prohibitive cost' of re-embedding/retraining at industrial (billions-scale) corpus sizes, and the scalability of the proposed training procedure to such settings is not discussed.

The method relies on a single rewriter backbone (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, with Qwen2-VL-7B for CIRR); no experiments vary the base LLM/VLM, so claims about general applicability of the ranking-reward framework across different rewriter architectures are unsupported.

Reported 'data efficiency' results (Fig. 4) use training sets as large as 100k-148k queries per dataset for the main results, yet the data-efficiency argument is based on subsampling this already large, task-specific, retrieval-aligned training corpus—such training data (paired query-image sets from the same distribution as the test set) may not be readily available in real cold-start deployments, limiting the practical relevance of the efficiency claim.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent notation (e.g., z_t vs z_i in Eq. 5), and overall the manuscript shows signs of inconsistent proofreading (duplicated algorithmic descriptions, awkward LaTeX rendering) that reduce confidence in the overall care taken in preparing the submission.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: adapting frozen CLIP retrievers to distribution-shifted queries (multilingual, long-form, multimodal) without costly retraining or re-embedding, which matters for large-scale deployed vector search systems.

The paper provides a clear and plausible analysis of the 'score inflation' phenomenon in similarity-based reward fine-tuning, supported by both a decomposition argument (shared-mean cancellation under ranking objectives) and empirical training curves showing similarity rising while Recall@1 falls (Fig. 5/6).

Broad empirical coverage across five benchmarks spanning three distinct distribution-shift categories, with three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), showing consistent relative improvements of +LLM over baseline and +GRAPE over +LLM.

Reasonably thorough ablations are included: data efficiency curves, robustness to group size K, failure-mode/hallucination auditing, long-query length-vs-performance decoupling analysis, and per-language breakdowns on XM3600 that honestly reveal where the method's gains shrink (low-resource languages).

Good reproducibility details for a short paper: explicit prompt templates, training hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and an affine-invariance derivation justifying the ranking-reward design choice.
weaknesses: The central claimed contribution (ranking reward vs. similarity reward / score inflation mitigation) is empirically demonstrated in detail on only one dataset (Flickr30k-CN); the 'CLIP+GRPO-LLM (similarity reward)' baseline described in Section 4.1 is never actually shown in the main results table (Table 1), so the paper's core comparison is not validated across the full benchmark suite.

No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere; all Recall numbers appear to be single-run point estimates, making it hard to judge whether the ~4-5% average gains are statistically robust, especially on smaller datasets like Wikipedia (2,173 train queries) and CIRR (3,336 queries).

The paper does not compare against trained multilingual/long-text CLIP variants discussed in related work (e.g., mCLIP, AltCLIP, Long-CLIP) even though these directly target the same distribution shifts; such a comparison would clarify how much performance GRAPE recovers relative to full retraining, which is the central motivating alternative.
CIRR is evaluated with a non-standard 80/20 train/validation split rather than the dataset's established protocol, without justification, limiting comparability to prior CIRR literature.

Training-time computational cost of the ranking reward is not analyzed: computing the full rank of the target image among N candidates for every one of K rewrites at every optimization step could be expensive for large corpora, yet the efficiency discussion (Section 5) only addresses inference latency, not training cost/scalability.

The appendix baseline comparison against 'Claude-Sonnet-4.6' and 'GPT-5.4' (Table 4) lacks citations/version details and is only reported on two datasets with a single data point each, which weakens confidence in this comparison and raises reproducibility concerns.

The manual failure-mode audit (Appendix A.6) is based on only 100 samples from a single dataset with no stated annotation protocol or inter-rater agreement, limiting the reliability of the 14%→3% failure-rate claim.

Group-wise reward normalization combines format-reward-skipped and retrieval-evaluated rewrites into the same group statistics (mean/std over K), but the paper does not clarify how non-conforming (format-failed, retrieval-skipped) samples are handled within the ranking-reward computation, which could introduce inconsistent group sizes/statistics across training steps.
